To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have designed and synthesized a second-generation 99Tc SPECT imaging agent, FLUORATECTM, that binds potently and selectively with the DAT in vitro and in vivo and provides a quantitative measure of the density of the DAT in vivo in nonhuman primate brain.
second-generation 99 m technetium-based tropanes have been developed and evaluated for in vivo imaging of the DAT.
we have developed a second-generation (99 m) technetium-based SPECT agent that provides in-vivo images of the dopamine transporters in primate brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing new radioligands for SPECT imaging of the DAT.
the discovery and development of new radiopharmaceuticals for the diagnosis of neurological diseases.
the discovery and development of radiolabeled compounds that bind to the DAT and are used as imaging agents for SPECT.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have designed and synthesized a second-generation (99)technetium based tropane ligand that is selective for the DAT, has improved biological stability, and is capable of labeling the DAT in the nonhuman primate.
the development of a second-generation (99)mtechnetium-based SPECT agent for the imaging of the DAT has been achieved.

the design, synthesis and in vivo imaging studies of second-generation (1R,3alpha)-3-(4-fluoro-phenyl)-8-(3-mercapto-propyl)-8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane derivatives have led to the identification of FLUORATECs as potent, selective, and biostable DAT imaging agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a second-generation (99)technetium DAT imaging agent that provides in vitro and in vivo images of DAT in primate brain and that this agent is now in human clinical trials.
a second-generation 99Tc-based DAT imaging agent was designed, synthesized, and evaluated in vivo in nonhuman primats.
a new generation of SPECT agents has been designed that are more selective for the DAT, more stable, and more potent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
second-generation (99)technetium tropane ligands can label the DAT in nonhuman primtes and that this approach can be translated to humans for the diagnosis of neurological disorders.
the DAT can be visualized with a second-generation (99)technetium SPECT agent in vivo in nonhuman primate brains.
the development of second-generation (1R)3alpha-(4-flourophenyl)tropanes has allowed for in vivo imaging of the DAT in nonhuman primmates.
